# MEMORANDUM

**To:** [Supervising Partner]
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 6, 2026
**Re:** Zaibeind Hospitality Partners, LLC: acquisition of The Larkspur House from Stavain Inn Holdings, LLC. Review of transaction documents and ranked issues list

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed the five documents in the matter folder:

- the Asset Purchase Agreement dated as of March 2, 2026 (the **APA**);
- the $3,200,000 Secured Promissory Note (the **Seller Note** or **Note**);
- the Seller Disclosure Schedule;
- the Bill of Sale and Assignment;
- the March 24, 2026 integration meeting notes.

The Bill of Sale and the Note both record that Closing occurred on **April 15, 2026**. The Note matures 36 months later, on April 15, 2029.

Three issues are significant for Zaibeind as Buyer and as Maker of the Note. I rank them as follows:

1. **Tax indemnity survival gap (APA §9.1, §1.1, Note §4).** All indemnity claims, including Seller's indemnity for Pre-Closing Taxes, expire nine months after Closing, on **January 15, 2027**. That is about ten weeks from today. The Note setoff right expires on the same date. New York can assess pre-closing sales and occupancy tax for roughly three years after the returns are filed. This issue is ranked first because it is time-critical.
2. **Uncapped assumption of Seller's pre-closing contract breaches (APA §2.3(a), §9.3(b), §9.5).** Zaibeind has assumed, and must indemnify Seller against, Seller's own pre-closing breaches of the Assigned Contracts, with no cap. This includes the disclosed **$410,000 Hudson Valley Wedding Collective claim**.
3. **Portfolio-wide "Business" definition in the Seller Note (Note §1.2, §6.2, §7.1(d); APA §11.9).** The Note's transfer and encumbrance covenant reaches every hotel owned, leased or managed by Zaibeind and its Affiliates. A breach permits acceleration of the full $3,200,000. Because the Note controls on Maker covenants and Events of Default, the narrower APA definition does not cure this.

Part IV covers several secondary points.

**Threshold fact to confirm.** The folder copies show blank signature blocks, but the Bill of Sale and Note recite that Closing occurred on April 15, 2026. If the documents were executed in this form, every fix below requires a written amendment signed by both parties (APA §11.4; Note §9.2), and Seller has little incentive to agree. Our recommendations therefore address both:

- what we can do unilaterally now, chiefly protective claim notices before January 15, 2027; and
- what we should seek by amendment.

We need to confirm with the client whether the executed versions match these drafts. We should also ask whether any side letters or amendments were signed at Closing.

---

## II. Ranked Issues

### Issue 1: Nine-month survival period cuts off Pre-Closing Tax indemnity and Note setoff

**Where:**
- APA §9.1 (Survival);
- APA §1.1 (definition of "Fundamental Representations");
- APA §4.12 (Taxes) and §2.4(a) / §9.2(b) (Pre-Closing Taxes as an Excluded Liability);
- Seller Note §4.1 (Setoff).

**What the documents say:**

- **APA §9.1 sets a single nine-month period.** The representations, warranties, covenants "and the indemnification obligations under Section 9.2" survive "until nine (9) months following the Closing Date." With Closing on April 15, 2026, the Survival Period ends **January 15, 2027**. The section also states that "No claim for indemnification under Section 9.2 may be made after the expiration of the applicable survival period."
- **The only carve-out is the Fundamental Representations.** These survive six years. The §1.1 definition covers only §4.1 (Organization), §4.2 (Authority) and §4.7 (Title). It does **not** include §4.12 (Taxes). In §4.12 Seller represents that it timely filed returns and collected and remitted New York State sales tax on hotel occupancy, food and beverage and the Columbia County hotel room occupancy tax. The §4.12 representation is therefore subject to the nine-month period like any other general representation.
- **The limit also reaches the Excluded Liabilities indemnity.** Section 9.1 applies the nine-month limit to "the indemnification obligations under Section 9.2" as a whole. So the cut-off is not confined to representation claims. It also covers Seller's **§9.2(b) indemnity for Excluded Liabilities**, which include all Pre-Closing Taxes (§2.4(a)). The Pre-Closing Taxes definition expressly includes hotel occupancy sales tax and the Columbia County occupancy tax. Section 9.5 removes §9.2(b) from the cap, but that does not help after the claim period has closed.
- **The Note setoff right ends on the same date.** Note §4.1 limits setoff "only to indemnity claims asserted in writing within the survival period set forth in Section 9.1 of the Purchase Agreement." APA §9.6 provides that setoff operates "on the terms set forth in the Seller Note."

**Why it matters to Zaibeind:**

- **Assessment timing.** New York sales and use tax (including tax on hotel occupancy) is generally assessable for three years after a return is filed. The period is longer, or unlimited, if no return was filed or the return was fraudulent. Seller's returns for the quarter that includes the April 15, 2026 Closing, and for earlier quarters, can be audited and assessed into 2029. Most of that window falls after January 15, 2027. The Columbia County occupancy tax is imposed under county local law, and we should confirm its assessment period.
- **Successor liability.** Under Tax Law §1141(c), a bulk-sale purchaser can become liable for the seller's unpaid sales taxes. This applies if the 10-day advance notice was not properly given, or if the Department served a notice of claim and the purchaser did not withhold. Hotel audits often focus on exempt-stay claims (permanent residents, government and tax-exempt guests), OTA merchant-model receipts and event and F&B receipts. Any assessment of that kind can fall on Zaibeind directly as the operator and successor.
- **Lost recourse and leverage.** After January 15, 2027, Zaibeind would bear that exposure with **no contractual indemnity** and **no right to set it off** against the $3,200,000 Note. The Note is Zaibeind's main practical leverage, because Seller sold substantially all its operating assets and may have distributed the cash proceeds.
- **No disclosed tax matters.** Schedule 4.12 reads "None," so no tax matter was carved out as pre-disclosed.

**Recommended fix:**

1. **Immediate step, which does not require Seller's consent.** Before January 15, 2027, deliver a written indemnity notice to Seller "with reasonable specificity" under §9.1 and §9.4.
   - The notice should assert claims under §9.2(a) (breach of §4.12) and §9.2(b) (Pre-Closing Taxes) for all pre-closing sales, use and occupancy tax periods.
   - It should identify the tax types, periods and the specific risk areas the client has found. Under §9.1, a claim asserted in this way "shall survive until finally resolved."
   - It should also expressly invoke Note §4.1, so the setoff right is preserved for claims asserted within the Survival Period.
   - Seller may argue that a contingent, unassessed claim is not "reasonably specific," so the more concrete the notice, the stronger it is. We should calendar a target of mid-December 2026.
2. **Amendment to seek.**
   - Amend §1.1 to add §4.12 to the Fundamental Representations, or create a separate survival tier for §4.12.
   - Amend §9.1 so that §4.12 and the §9.2(b) indemnity for Pre-Closing Taxes (and Excluded Liabilities generally) survive until **60 days after expiration of the applicable statute of limitations, including extensions and waivers**.
   - Conform Note §4.1 so that setoff is available for any claim asserted within the applicable survival period for that claim, not only the general §9.1 period.
3. **If Seller will not amend.** Consider whether to commission a pre-January 2027 sales and occupancy tax review of Seller's returns. This would let us convert contingent exposure into specific claims while the window is open.

**Facts to confirm with the client:**

- Was the §1141(c) bulk sale notice (Form AU-196.10) actually filed at least 10 days before Closing? The meeting notes target April 3, 2026, and APA §3.2(g) required evidence of filing. Did the Department issue a notice of claim, and did Zaibeind withhold or escrow any of the purchase price in response?
- Has Zaibeind received any audit contact, notice or inquiry from the Department of Taxation and Finance or Columbia County about pre-closing periods?
- What is Seller's tax filing history: quarterly or annual filer, any late filings? Did Zaibeind's diligence identify any exempt-stay or OTA-related concerns?
- Did Zaibeind file its own Certificate of Authority and county occupancy registration effective at Closing, as the meeting notes contemplated? This tells us how cleanly the periods are separated.

---

### Issue 2: Uncapped assumption of, and indemnity for, Seller's pre-closing contract breaches

**Where:**
- APA §2.3(a) (Assumed Liabilities);
- APA §2.4 (Excluded Liabilities);
- APA §9.3(b) (Buyer indemnity for Assumed Liabilities);
- APA §9.5 (Limitations);
- Disclosure Schedule 2.1(c) item 1, 4.4 item 1, 4.9 item 1 and 4.10 item 1.

**What the documents say:**

- **Assumed Liabilities include pre-closing obligations.** Section 2.3(a) makes Assumed Liabilities "all liabilities and obligations arising under the Assigned Contracts, **whether arising before or after the Closing**."
- **No carve-back.** Section 2.4 makes Seller retain everything other than Assumed Liabilities, but lists nothing that pulls Seller's pre-closing contract breaches back out of §2.3(a).
- **Buyer indemnifies Seller.** Section 9.3(b) requires Zaibeind to indemnify Seller against all Losses arising from any Assumed Liability.
- **No cap.** Section 9.5 caps each party's liability at 10% of the Purchase Price ($1,840,000) but states that the limitations "**shall not apply to claims under Section 9.2(b) or Section 9.3(b)**." The §9.3(b) exposure therefore has no limit.
- **Seller's reciprocal indemnity does not help.** Seller's uncapped §9.2(b) indemnity covers only Excluded Liabilities, and these pre-closing contract breaches are not Excluded Liabilities.

**Why it matters to Zaibeind:**

- **The Hudson Valley Wedding Collective claim falls on Zaibeind.**
  - Schedule 2.1(c) lists the Hudson Valley Wedding Collective Room Block and Event Services Agreement as an Assigned Contract.
  - Schedule 4.9 discloses that Seller cancelled the June 12–14, 2026 room block (38 rooms, two nights) and garden pavilion block by notice dated March 1, 2026.
  - Schedule 4.10 discloses a **$410,000** demand for liquidated cancellation fees, vendor deposit reimbursement and lost commissions, with a threatened Columbia County Supreme Court action.
  - Under §2.3(a) that liability is an Assumed Liability. Zaibeind must pay it and also indemnify Seller for it, including Seller's defense costs, with no cap.
- **Zaibeind has no representation claim either.** The breach was disclosed on Schedule 4.9 and Schedule 4.10, so it is carved out of the §4.9 and §4.10 representations. The cancellation (March 1) also predates the §5.1 conduct-of-business covenant, which ran from the Effective Date of March 2.
- **The same structure applies across all 13 Assigned Contracts.** These include the OTA agreements (chargebacks, rate parity, commission true-ups), vendor contracts and the late-paid Valley Linen invoice on Schedule 4.9 item 2. Every unknown pre-closing breach is Zaibeind's, uncapped.

**Recommended fix:**

1. **Amendment.**
   - Revise §2.3(a) to read "all liabilities and obligations arising under the Assigned Contracts **to the extent arising out of or relating to periods after the Closing**, excluding any liability arising out of any breach or default by Seller occurring on or before the Closing."
   - Add a new §2.4(h) making "all liabilities arising out of any breach of or default under any Assigned Contract occurring on or before the Closing, **including the matters described on Schedules 4.9 and 4.10**" an Excluded Liability. That brings these liabilities under Seller's uncapped §9.2(b) indemnity.
   - Expressly name the Hudson Valley Wedding Collective claim as an Excluded Liability.
2. **Coordinate with Issue 1.** Make sure the §9.2(b) indemnity for this new Excluded Liability is not itself cut off on January 15, 2027.
3. **If Seller will not amend.** Consider these alternative arguments, none of which is strong on the drafting as it stands:
   - that the Collective's claim "arises under" Seller's cancellation as a pre-closing tort or business matter rather than under the contract;
   - whether the agreement was in fact assigned (see the consent question below);
   - a negotiated price reduction or setoff by agreement.
4. **Control the claim.** Zaibeind is the economic party in interest. It should control, or at least closely monitor, Seller's handling of the Collective claim. Section 9.4 gives the Indemnifying Party (here, Zaibeind) the right to assume the defense.

**Facts to confirm with the client:**

- Was the Hudson Valley Wedding Collective's consent to assignment (Schedule 4.4 item 1) obtained? The meeting notes show it outstanding as of March 24. If the agreement was never assigned, there is a stronger argument that its liabilities did not pass to Zaibeind.
- What is the current status of the $410,000 claim? Has suit been filed, has Seller tendered it to Zaibeind, has anything been paid or settled, and has Seller's insurer been notified?
- Did the client price or reserve for this claim, or have any side understanding with Seller about it?
- Is the client aware of other pre-closing disputes under the OTA, vendor or group contracts?

---

### Issue 3: Seller Note defines "Business" to cover Zaibeind's entire portfolio, and the Note controls on covenants and defaults

**Where:**
- Seller Note §1.2 (definition of "Business");
- Note §6.2 (Restrictions on Transfer and Encumbrance);
- Note §7.1(d) and §7.2 (Event of Default; Acceleration);
- APA §1.1 (definition of "Business");
- APA §11.9 (Order of Precedence).

**What the documents say:**

- **Two different definitions.** APA §1.1 defines "Business" as "the ownership and operation of the Hotel by Seller." Note §1.2 instead defines it as "**all hotels and hospitality operations owned, leased or managed by Maker or any of its Affiliates**."
- **The covenant.** Note §6.2 prohibits Maker, and Maker "shall not permit any of its Affiliates," without Holder's prior written consent, to "sell, transfer, lease, refinance or encumber any material portion of the assets of the Business." The only exceptions are ordinary-course inventory and FF&E, the Senior Indebtedness lien and the Mortgage.
- **The default.** Under Note §7.1(d), any breach of §6.2 is an immediate Event of Default, with no notice or cure period, unlike §7.1(c). Section 7.2 then lets Holder accelerate the full $3,200,000 plus interest. The Default Rate is 10% per annum (6% + 4%).
- **Which document controls.** APA §11.9 generally makes the APA control over Ancillary Documents, "**except that the Seller Note shall control as to payment terms, Maker covenants and Events of Default**." Section 6.2 is a Maker covenant and §7.1(d) is an Event of Default. The Note's broader definition therefore governs those provisions, and the APA's Hotel-only definition does not override it.

**Why it matters to Zaibeind:**

- **Seller gains a veto over unrelated hotels.** Any refinancing, sale, ground lease, sale-leaseback or new mortgage on **any other hotel** owned, leased or managed by Zaibeind or any Affiliate needs Seller's consent for as long as the Note is outstanding, until April 15, 2029. Seller is an unrelated former owner, and the restriction gives it a hold-up right over transactions that have nothing to do with The Larkspur House.
- **Acceleration and cross-default risk.** A portfolio transaction done without consent would be an immediate Event of Default. That could trigger acceleration and Default Rate interest, and possibly cross-defaults under Zaibeind's senior or other financing.
- **The covenant is not limited to Larkspur's financing.** The Senior Indebtedness exception covers only the Hotel's acquisition financing, so the covenant is not cut back to it.
- **Possible existing defaults.** If any Affiliate has already refinanced or sold a property since April 15, 2026, Zaibeind may already be in default.

**Recommended fix:**

1. **Amendment.** Conform the Note definition to the APA: "'Business' means the ownership and operation of the Hotel." Alternatively, delete the Note definition and rely on the §1.2 incorporation of APA definitions. Limit §6.2 to the Hotel and the Real Property, and delete "or any of its Affiliates" and "shall not permit any of its Affiliates."
2. **Related changes to seek at the same time:**
   - add a notice and cure period to §7.1(d);
   - expand the §6.2 exceptions to permit refinancing of the Senior Indebtedness generally, subject to the senior/subordinate intercreditor terms.
3. **Amend APA §11.9 as a backstop**, so that defined terms in the APA control over any inconsistent definition in an Ancillary Document.
4. **Interim position.** Until an amendment is signed, the client should treat any Affiliate-level disposition or financing as requiring Seller's consent. Alternatively, it could prepay the Note, which Note §3 permits without premium.

**Facts to confirm with the client:**

- Which hotels and hospitality operations do Zaibeind and its Affiliates own, lease or manage? Which entities count as "Affiliates" under common control?
- Since April 15, 2026, has any Affiliate sold, refinanced, leased or encumbered a material portion of any hotel's assets? Are any such transactions planned before April 2029?
- Do Zaibeind's senior or other credit facilities contain cross-default provisions triggered by an Event of Default under the Seller Note?
- Is early prepayment of the Note a realistic option, given that it would remove the covenant entirely?

---

## III. Interaction Among the Issues

The three issues reinforce each other.

- **The Note is the client's leverage.** The Note setoff is Zaibeind's main protection against Seller. Issue 1 ends setoff for tax claims in January 2027, and §4.2 already restricts setoff to amounts "finally determined" by agreement or non-appealable judgment.
- **The Note is also Seller's leverage.** Issue 3 gives Seller a portfolio-wide acceleration right that it could use against Zaibeind in any indemnity dispute.
- **The Collective claim does not fit the setoff at all.** Under Issue 2, the $410,000 claim flows the wrong way: Zaibeind owes the indemnity, so there is nothing to set off.

We should raise all three together in a single amendment request, using the Issue 3 consent dynamics and the client's prepayment option as negotiating context.

---

## IV. Secondary Points

These are lower priority but worth addressing in any amendment or confirming with the client.

1. **Setoff mechanics (Note §4.2).** Setoff is available only for amounts agreed in writing or reduced to a final, non-appealable judgment. Contested claims cannot be withheld while they are pending. *Fix:* permit Maker to withhold, or pay into escrow, amounts subject to a good-faith pending claim, without that being an Event of Default.
2. **Bulk sale notice (APA §5.5, §3.2(g)).**
   - Section 5.5 frames the §1141(c) notice as Seller's cooperation obligation. Under the statute, however, the notice is the purchaser's obligation, and the purchaser's exposure is what turns on it.
   - Section 3.2(g) is also garbled: "evidence that Seller has filed Form AU-196.10 ... has been delivered."
   - These matter only if the notice was not timely filed. See the questions under Issue 1.
3. **Cap and basket on tax representation claims (APA §9.5).** A §4.12 claim brought under §9.2(a) is subject to the $92,000 basket and the $1,840,000 cap. Only the §9.2(b) Pre-Closing Taxes route is uncapped. Any amendment should make clear that tax claims are uncapped whichever route is used.
4. **Seller creditworthiness.** Seller sold substantially all its operating assets. Beyond the Note, there is no escrow, holdback or parent guaranty supporting Seller's indemnities. We should ask the client whether Seller has distributed the $15,200,000 cash proceeds. If our leverage allows, we should seek a guaranty or escrow in exchange for the amendments Seller may want.
5. **Integration meeting notes (March 24, 2026).** The notes are an internal operational document and create no contractual issues of their own. They are useful mainly as a record of items to confirm, such as Hudson Valley Wedding Collective consent, the bulk sale filing, and Buyer's sales tax and occupancy tax registrations. They also confirm the April 15, 2026 Closing and the $15,200,000 / $3,200,000 split.

---

## V. Recommended Next Steps

1. **By mid-December 2026:** serve a protective §9.1 / §9.4 indemnity notice covering Pre-Closing Taxes and the §4.12 representation. The notice should expressly preserve Note §4.1 setoff (Issue 1).
2. **Now:** gather the client facts listed above, starting with:
   - whether the executed documents match these drafts;
   - bulk sale filing status;
   - Hudson Valley Wedding Collective consent and claim status;
   - any Affiliate transactions since Closing.
3. **Prepare an omnibus amendment to the APA and the Note covering:**
   - extended tax survival and conforming setoff (Issue 1);
   - limiting §2.3(a) and adding the new §2.4(h) Excluded Liability (Issue 2);
   - conforming the Note's "Business" definition and adding a §7.1(d) cure period (Issue 3);
   - the §4.2 setoff and escrow mechanics.
4. **Evaluate with the client** whether early prepayment of the Note is preferable to negotiating Issue 3, weighing that against the loss of setoff leverage under Issue 1.

Please let me know if you would like me to draft the claim notice or the amendment.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 6, 2026
**Re:** Zaibeind Hospitality Partners, LLC: acquisition of The Larkspur House from Stavain Inn Holdings, LLC. Issues review of transaction documents.

**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## I. Background and Scope

Zaibeind Hospitality Partners, LLC ("**Zaibeind**" or "**Buyer**") acquired substantially all the assets of The Larkspur House, a 42-room boutique hotel at 214 Warren Street, Hudson, New York. The seller was Stavain Inn Holdings, LLC ("**Seller**"). The deal was made under an Asset Purchase Agreement dated as of March 2, 2026 (the "**APA**"), governed by New York law (APA § 11.6).

- **Purchase Price:** $18,400,000 (APA § 2.5).
  - $15,200,000 paid in cash at Closing.
  - **$3,200,000** deferred through a Secured Promissory Note issued by Zaibeind as Maker to Seller as Holder (the "**Seller Note**"). The Note bears 6.0% interest and matures 36 months after Closing.
- **Closing Date:** **April 15, 2026**, per Bill of Sale § 1.2 and the Seller Note.

I reviewed the following documents:
- the APA;
- the Seller Note;
- the Seller Disclosure Schedule;
- the Bill of Sale and Assignment; and
- the March 24, 2026 integration meeting notes.

The meeting notes are internal operational notes. They contain no operative terms. I used them only to cross-check facts such as the Closing timeline, the consents and the tax registrations.

**Timing point.** The Bill of Sale and Note are dated April 15, 2026, so the transaction appears to have closed on these forms. If so, the "fixes" below must be done by negotiated amendment, side letter, or protective action. Some are now time-critical: **the general survival period expires January 15, 2027, about ten weeks from today.** We should confirm with the client that the executed versions match the folder copies.

The issues are ranked by significance to Zaibeind as Buyer and Note Maker.

---

## II. Summary of Issues

| Rank | Issue | Location | Exposure |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Nine-month survival cuts off tax indemnity and Note setoff for pre-closing sales/occupancy taxes | APA § 9.1, § 1.1 ("Fundamental Representations"); Seller Note § 4.1 | Open-ended pre-closing tax and successor liability. Deadline: January 15, 2027 |
| 2 | Pre-closing Assigned Contract liabilities are Assumed Liabilities, and Buyer's indemnity for them is uncapped | APA §§ 2.3(a), 2.4, 9.3(b), 9.5 | Uncapped. Includes the $410,000 Hudson Valley Wedding Collective claim |
| 3 | Note setoff requires a "final, non-appealable judgment" | Seller Note §§ 4.1–4.2; APA § 9.6 | Setoff is practically unusable within the Note's life |
| 4 | Bulk-sale compliance and successor sales tax liability | APA §§ 3.2(g), 5.5; Tax Law § 1141(c) | Personal successor liability for Seller's unpaid sales tax |
| 5 | Hudson Valley Wedding Collective consent and assignment status | Disclosure Schedule 4.4(1), 4.9(1), 4.10(1) | Bears on how Issue 2 plays out |
| 6 | Drafting and lesser points | APA § 3.2(g); Seller Note "Senior Indebtedness" definition; Disclosure Schedule 4.12 | Low to moderate |

---

## III. Issues

### Issue 1: Survival gap for pre-closing hotel sales and occupancy taxes

**Where:**
- APA § 9.1 (Survival);
- APA § 1.1, definition of "Fundamental Representations";
- APA § 4.12 (Taxes); §§ 2.4(a) and 9.2(b);
- Seller Note § 4.1 (Right of Setoff).

**What the documents say.**

- **Survival.** APA § 9.1 provides that the representations, warranties, covenants and agreements, "and the indemnification obligations under Section 9.2, shall survive the Closing until **nine (9) months following the Closing Date**." Measured from the April 15, 2026 Closing Date, the Survival Period ends **January 15, 2027**. No § 9.2 claim may be made after that date unless it was asserted in writing with reasonable specificity beforehand.
- **Fundamental Representations.** The only exception is for Fundamental Representations, which survive six years. Section 1.1 limits these to § 4.1 (Organization), § 4.2 (Authority) and § 4.7 (Title). **The § 4.12 tax representation is not a Fundamental Representation.** It therefore survives only the nine-month general period. Section 4.12 covers timely filing, collection and remittance of New York State sales tax on hotel occupancy and F&B receipts, and the Columbia County hotel room occupancy tax.
- **Excluded Liabilities indemnity.** Section 9.1 applies the nine-month limit to "the indemnification obligations under Section 9.2" as a whole. That captures **Seller's § 9.2(b) indemnity for Excluded Liabilities**, which include all Pre-Closing Taxes under § 2.4(a). Pre-Closing Taxes are expressly defined to include New York State sales and use taxes on hotel occupancy and the Columbia County occupancy tax. Section 9.5 carves § 9.2(b) out of the cap and basket, but that does not help once the claim is time-barred.
- **Note setoff.** Seller Note § 4.1 confines Maker's setoff right to "indemnity claims asserted in writing within the survival period set forth in Section 9.1 of the Purchase Agreement."

**Why it matters to Zaibeind.**

- **Assessment window.** New York may generally assess sales and use tax within three years after a return is filed (Tax Law § 1147(b)). There is no limit where no return was filed or where a return was willfully false. The last pre-closing sales tax period is the March–May 2026 quarter, with the short pre-closing stub ending April 14/15. That return was due in June 2026. The State therefore can assess pre-closing hotel sales tax until roughly mid-2029. The Columbia County occupancy tax likely follows a similar audit cycle; this needs to be confirmed against the county local law.
- **Successor liability.** As a bulk purchaser, Zaibeind can face direct successor liability for Seller's unpaid sales taxes under Tax Law § 1141(c) (see Issue 4).
- **Effect of the documents together.** An assessment issued after January 15, 2027 would leave Zaibeind with:
  - no indemnity under § 9.2(a) (rep breach) or § 9.2(b) (Excluded Liability);
  - no setoff against the $3,200,000 Note, its natural security for this exposure; and
  - under § 9.7, no other contractual remedy short of proving fraud.
- **Wider reach of the cutoff.** The same cutoff also ends Seller's indemnity for every other Excluded Liability. These include pre-closing employment/WARN liabilities (§ 2.4(d)), benefit plan liabilities (§ 2.4(e)) and pre-closing environmental liabilities (§ 2.4(f)), which commonly surface well after nine months.
- **Scale.** At 42 rooms, combined sales and occupancy tax on room revenue alone can be material across a three-year lookback, before penalties and interest.

**Recommended fix.**

1. **Amend APA § 9.1** (by amendment if closed) so that:
   - § 4.12 survives until 60 days after expiration of the applicable statute of limitations, including extensions and waivers. Alternatively, add § 4.12 to the "Fundamental Representations" definition and give it a statute-of-limitations-plus-60-days survival rather than six years.
   - The § 9.2(b) Excluded Liabilities indemnity is carved out of the nine-month limit entirely, or at minimum survives until 60 days after the applicable limitations period for the underlying liability.
2. **Conform Seller Note § 4.1** so that setoff applies to any indemnity claim asserted within the *applicable* survival period, not only "the survival period set forth in Section 9.1."
3. **Interim protective step (time-critical).** If an amendment cannot be agreed before January 15, 2027, send Seller a written § 9.1/§ 9.4 claim notice before that date. The notice should describe with reasonable specificity potential Pre-Closing Tax liabilities for all pre-closing periods, along with the other Excluded Liabilities. A claim "asserted in writing with reasonable specificity" before expiration survives until resolved under § 9.1 and preserves Note § 4.1 setoff. Seller may argue a generic "protective" notice is not "reasonably specific," so the notice should identify the tax types, jurisdictions and periods.
4. **Consider a tax escrow or holdback** from Note payments in exchange for any concessions on the above.

**Facts to confirm with the client:**
- Whether the APA and Note were executed in this form, and whether any side letter altered survival.
- Whether Zaibeind or its tax advisors did tax diligence on Seller's sales and occupancy tax filings. Was there any history of late filing, audits or voluntary disclosures? (Schedule 4.12 says "None.")
- The filing frequency of Seller's sales tax returns (quarterly or monthly) and the date of Seller's final return, so we can compute the actual limitations dates.
- Whether any DTF or Columbia County notice or audit inquiry has been received since Closing.

---

### Issue 2: Uncapped Buyer liability for Seller's pre-closing contract breaches

**Where:**
- APA § 2.3(a) (Assumed Liabilities);
- APA § 2.4 (Excluded Liabilities);
- APA § 9.3(b) (Buyer indemnity);
- APA § 9.5 (Limitations).

**What the documents say.**

- **Assumed Liabilities.** Section 2.3(a) makes Assumed Liabilities "all liabilities and obligations arising under the Assigned Contracts, **whether arising before or after the Closing**."
- **No carve-back.** Section 2.4 contains no carve-back for Seller's pre-closing breaches of Assigned Contracts.
- **Buyer indemnity.** Section 9.3(b) requires Buyer to indemnify Seller for all Losses arising from any Assumed Liability.
- **Cap carve-out.** Section 9.5 caps each party at 10% of the Purchase Price ($1,840,000), but provides that the limitations "**shall not apply to claims under Section 9.2(b) or Section 9.3(b)**."

**Why it matters to Zaibeind.**

- **Uncapped exposure.** Zaibeind has contractually taken on, without cap, liability for Seller's own pre-closing breaches of every Assigned Contract on Schedule 2.1(c). That list covers three group/room-block agreements, three OTA agreements, four vendor agreements and three equipment/software agreements. Zaibeind must also indemnify Seller, uncapped, if the counterparty pursues Seller.
- **Seller's indemnity does not help.** Seller's own uncapped § 9.2(b) indemnity covers only Excluded Liabilities, so it is no protection here.
- **Rep claims are blocked.** A rep-based claim under § 9.2(a) is also blocked. Seller disclosed the breach on Schedule 4.9, so § 4.9 is not inaccurate. Any rep claim would in any event be capped and subject to the nine-month survival (Issue 1).
- **The exposure is concrete:**
  - Schedule 2.1(c)(1) lists the **Hudson Valley Wedding Collective Agreement** as an Assigned Contract.
  - Schedule 4.9(1) discloses that on March 1, 2026, Seller cancelled the June 12–14, 2026 block of 38 rooms and the garden pavilion.
  - Schedule 4.10(1) discloses a **$410,000** demand for liquidated cancellation fees, vendor deposit reimbursement and lost commissions, with a threatened Columbia County Supreme Court action.
  - Under § 2.3(a), that liability is Zaibeind's if the contract was assigned.
  - The cancellation pre-dated the March 2 Effective Date, so Seller's § 5.1 covenant not to terminate Assigned Contracts without Buyer consent does not reach it.
- **Second disclosed item.** Schedule 4.9(2) discloses a late payment to Valley Linen Supply. This is minor, but it falls in the same category.

**Recommended fix.**

1. **Amend § 2.3(a)** to read: "all liabilities and obligations under the Assigned Contracts to the extent arising from and relating to periods after the Closing, *excluding* any liability arising out of any breach or default by Seller occurring on or before the Closing."
2. **Add a new § 2.4(h)** to the Excluded Liabilities: "all liabilities arising out of any breach of, default under, or cancellation or termination of any Assigned Contract by Seller on or before the Closing, including all liabilities under the Hudson Valley Wedding Collective Agreement relating to the June 12–14, 2026 event block and the claim described on Schedule 4.10, item 1." This places these liabilities under Seller's uncapped § 9.2(b) indemnity. That indemnity should in turn survive under the fix to Issue 1.
3. **Alternatively or additionally,** carve § 9.3(b) out of the cap exception to the extent the Losses arise from Seller's pre-closing conduct.
4. **For the Collective claim specifically,** seek:
   - Seller's acknowledgment that it retains the claim and will defend and settle it at its own cost; and
   - an express Note setoff right for any amount Zaibeind pays.

**Facts to confirm with the client:**
- Whether Hudson Valley Wedding Collective consented and the agreement was actually assigned at Closing. The March 24 notes show consent still outstanding. If it was not assigned, it may not be an Assigned Contract at all, which changes the analysis (see Issue 5).
- The current status of the $410,000 claim. The 45-day demand window from March 2 ran out around April 16, 2026. Was suit filed, against whom, and has anyone tendered defense to Zaibeind?
- Whether Zaibeind has received any demands from other Assigned Contract counterparties (OTAs, vendors, Catskill Arts Retreats, Rivertown) relating to pre-closing periods.
- Whether there was any side agreement or purchase price adjustment that took account of the Collective claim.

### Issue 3: Note setoff mechanics are too restrictive to be useful

**Where:** Seller Note §§ 4.1–4.3; APA § 9.6.

**What the documents say.** Setoff is limited to amounts "finally determined." Under § 4.2, that means either (a) Holder's written agreement or (b) "a final, non-appealable judgment." APA § 9.6 echoes the requirement.

**Why it matters.**
- Seller controls option (a).
- Option (b) will rarely arrive within the Note's 36-month term for a contested tax or contract claim, given the exclusive New York County forum (APA § 11.7).
- In practice, Zaibeind must keep paying the Note while a claim is pending. If it withholds without a final determination, it risks an Event of Default under Note § 7.1(a)/(b), with Default Rate interest and acceleration.
- The Note's value as security for the Issue 1 and Issue 2 exposures is therefore largely illusory.

**Recommended fix.** Amend Note § 4 to allow Maker either to withhold, or to pay into a third-party escrow, the amount of any pending indemnity claim asserted in good faith. The amount would be released on final determination. Withholding or escrowing under this mechanism should not be an Event of Default. Any such amendment must be cleared against the Senior Lender's subordination terms.

**Facts to confirm:** Whether a subordination agreement with the Senior Lender has been signed (Note § 8), and whether it restricts amendments to the Note's payment or setoff terms.

### Issue 4: Bulk-sale compliance and successor sales tax liability

**Where:** APA § 5.5 (Bulk Sale Notice); APA § 3.2(g); New York Tax Law § 1141(c).

**What the documents say.**
- Section 5.5 requires notice to DTF at least ten days before Closing, with Seller to "cooperate."
- The integration notes target filing on April 3, 2026, which is twelve days before Closing.

**Why it matters.**
- **Buyer bears the obligation.** Under § 1141(c), the obligation to notify DTF falls on the *purchaser*. Failure to notify makes the purchaser personally liable for the seller's unpaid sales taxes.
- **Escrow requirement.** Even where notice is given, DTF may respond with a notice of claim. Once that occurs, the purchaser must withhold the consideration up to the claimed amount, or become liable for it.
- **Interaction with the Note.** The Note's deferred $3,200,000 is "consideration" for this purpose. A DTF claim served after Closing could require Zaibeind to withhold Note payments. Nothing in the Note expressly permits that, and doing so could be characterized as a payment default.
- **Interaction with Issue 1.** Any successor liability Zaibeind bears would be recoverable from Seller only through the time-limited indemnity in Issue 1.

**Recommended fix.**
1. Confirm the Form AU-196.10 was filed timely by Buyer and determine what DTF response was received (a release, or a notice of claim requiring escrow).
2. Add a Note provision that any amount withheld or paid to a taxing authority under Tax Law § 1141(c) or a comparable county provision is a permitted reduction of the Note and not an Event of Default.

**Facts to confirm with the client:**
- The date the bulk-sale notice was filed and by whom.
- Whether DTF issued a notice of claim or a release.
- Whether any amounts were withheld at Closing.

### Issue 5: Status of the Hudson Valley Wedding Collective consent

**Where:** Disclosure Schedule 4.4(1), 4.9(1) and 4.10(1); APA §§ 2.1(c), 5.3 and 7.1.

**What the documents show.** Assignment of the Collective agreement required the counterparty's consent. Consent was still outstanding as of the March 24 meeting.

**Why it matters.**
- The APA has no provision for how non-assignable contracts are treated if consent is not obtained. There is no "held in trust" or back-to-back mechanism.
- If the contract was nonetheless purported to be assigned, Zaibeind may have assumed the $410,000 liability under § 2.3(a) without obtaining the contract rights cleanly.
- If the contract was not assigned, Zaibeind should take the position that it is not an Assigned Contract and that the liability stayed with Seller as an Excluded Liability.

**Recommended fix.** Determine the actual status. If the contract was not assigned, document by side letter that it is excluded and that Seller retains all liability under it.

**Facts to confirm:** Whether consent was obtained, and whether the contract appears in the executed Assignment and Assumption of Assigned Contracts.

### Issue 6: Drafting and lesser points

**(a) APA § 3.2(g) is garbled.** It reads "evidence that Seller has filed Form AU-196.10 ... has been delivered." It also misattributes the filing to Seller, when the statutory obligation is the purchaser's. This is low risk post-closing, but it should be corrected in any amendment.

**(b) Seller Note "Senior Indebtedness" definition.** The subordination covers a refinancing only "in a principal amount not exceeding the outstanding principal amount being refinanced." A future upsized refinancing of the Hotel would therefore not be senior to the Note in the excess amount. Senior lenders typically will not accept that.
- **Fix:** Add a cushion, for example 110% plus costs, or a cap tied to loan-to-value.
- **To confirm:** Zaibeind's refinancing plans for the Hotel.

**(c) Disclosure Schedule 4.12: "None."** This is helpful as a rep. Under Issue 1, however, it has value only until January 15, 2027. It reinforces the need to extend § 4.12 survival.

**(d) Seller Note § 7.1(e) cross-default.** Acceleration of the Senior Indebtedness is an Event of Default under the Note. This is customary and acceptable. The client should simply be aware of it.
